title: Home as a small sanctuary
hookLine: a shelf, a candle, a book: Daniel's open window, and Ezekiel's little sanctuary
tomorrow: some people brought Jesus the day's bad news. what did he do with it?

lines: A SHELF, A CANDLE, A BOOK.
NO PETITION BUT TO THE KING.
cards: A shelf, a candle, a book. Some people keep a corner like that. The Book of Daniel tells about a corner with a window.
The king has signed a decree: for thirty days, no one may ask a petition of any god or man except the king. Daniel knows it's signed.

And then: "he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime."

teach.b: As he did aforetime. That's the answer. Daniel didn't open the window to make a point.
The window was already where he prayed: a room, a direction, three times a day.

teach.h: A HABIT BEFORE IT WAS A RISK.
teach.b: The corner was a habit long before it was a risk. He's caught, and thrown into the den, and in the morning he tells the king that God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths.
Jewish practice keeps both pieces of the picture.

teach.h: PRAY IN A ROOM WITH WINDOWS.
teach.b: Prayer faces toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud says a person should pray in a room with windows, pointing to Daniel. Even the phrase small sanctuary has a source.
Speaking to exiles far from the Temple, God says through Ezekiel: "yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come."
The rabbis read that little sanctuary as the synagogue and the house of study, holy places small enough to carry into exile.
So a corner at home isn't decoration. It's where the habit lives, so it's already there on the day you need it.

how: Jews pray facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud, pointing to Daniel, teaches praying in a room with windows; people on other paths keep a small corner at home for prayer or quiet.

games.q: what does “home as a small sanctuary” mean?
o: a small set place at home kept for quiet or prayer
a room in the house that only clergy may enter
a safe room for storing valuables during storms

p: no petition but to the king

s: Daniel opened his window to defy the king
he prayed there as he did aforetime. the habit came first.
the Talmud points to Daniel when it says to pray in a room with windows
his open window became a teaching.
Daniel prayed in secret so no one would see
his windows were open, toward Jerusalem.

games.q: your dad wants a quiet corner but says he'll set it up when the house is less busy. what does Daniel's story suggest?
o: start now; Daniel's window held because the habit was already there.
wait; a sanctuary needs a calm house before it can mean anything.
make it big and formal so the whole family takes it seriously.
games.why: Daniel prayed at his window as he did aforetime: when the hard day came, the place was already there.

practice: Choose one object for a corner of your home: a book, a stone, a candle, a photo. Look at it for a while. Decide where it will sit, and which way you'll face when you sit beside it.

wordCard.voice: Home as a small sanctuary: a corner where the habit lives, like Daniel's window, open toward Jerusalem on ordinary days.

orig.note: Hebrew: a little sanctuary (Ezekiel 11:16); the rabbis applied it to places of prayer and study.

carryVoice: Keep this one: my corner, open on easy days and hard ones, like Daniel's window. A week at home, done.

sources.q: he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.

sources.ref: Daniel 6:7-9, 16-22 (the thirty-day decree; the den; the angel shut the lions' mouths)

sources.q: yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b (pray only in a house with windows, from Daniel 6:10); Megillah 29a (the little sanctuary as synagogues and houses of study)
